newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD tries to force the pace on tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: German SPD tries to force the pace on tax cuts.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), looking ahead to general elections next year, sought on Friday to outflank the ruling coalition's plans to slash income tax in 1999 by calling for cuts a year earlier.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said reform plans announced by Finance Minister Theo Waigel would punish workers, pensioners and the unemployed. He called for urgent cross-party talks on cutting taxes from the start of 1998.

"We want to see a real impact on people's wallets in 1998, and not just promises of tax cuts for 1999," Lafontaine said, warning that if Chancellor Helmut Kohl wins election for a record fifth term his government would break its tax pledges.

The SPD chief was reacting to plans announced by Waigel to slash income and corporate taxes while scrapping over 70 tax breaks in measures that would leave taxpayers 30 billion marks ($18.31 billion) better off. The bulk of the cuts would come in 1999.

Waigel, hailing the reform proposal as cutting German tax rates to the lowest level since World War Two, said on Thursday it would boost investment and job creation, and speed economic growth by half a percentage point a year.

The reforms would slash income taxes in 1999, bringing in a starting rate of 15 percent, to be followed by a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent to 39 percent. Corporate taxes would fall in two steps with a new top rate of 35 percent.
Waigel wants to raise the 15 percent rate of VAT by one point to finance the cuts, but the SPD is threatening to veto such a rise in parliament's upper house, which it controls.

Plans to raise taxes on pensions and life insurance have also split Kohl's own Christian Democrat party (CDU). Labour Minister Norbert Bluem on Thursday was among a minority of CDU leaders who voted against the tax plan.
Kohl has ordered a cooling-off period before his party looks at the VAT issue again next month. Newspapers said he read the riot act to Bluem at a party meeting on Thursday.
While industry groups welcomed the plan's goal of slashing corporate taxation, other lobbies have been hostile.
Trade unions said that the abolition of tax breaks would hit the poor hardest, while the wealthy would win out from the lower top rate of tax.

That view was backed up by a survey by the Forsa institute which found that 62 percent of Germans thought they would not profit from the reform, and 64 percent thought the rich would benefit most. The survey sample was 500 people.
Commentators were also critical, with the Handelsblatt daily saying Waigel had fallen short of his goal of cutting top income tax to 35 percent from today's 53 percent.
"It is understandable that the coalition is trying to sell the tax reform as the work of the century. But its is not a convincing showpiece," Handelsblatt remarked.
The tax proposals face a long road before they become law.
Legislation is only expected to be introduced to parliament this summer. If the SPD blocks the measures a compromise may be delayed into early 1998 -- with autumn polls already looming.
But Kohl's lieutenant, CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, said he did not expect the plan to be watered down.
"A majority of the Bundesrat cannot reject this measure if it is aware of its duty to society," he said on Thursday. "I am optimistic we can win a majority in both houses of parliament."
